title.narrative: Improving source-to-sea governance to reduce the drivers of land-based impacts on the Large Marine Ecosystems in the SICA region

description.narrative: 338. The CAM Project generates regional co-benefits by advancing a sustainable blue and green economy across the SICA countries. By reducing land-based sources of pollution flowing into coastal and marine environments through an integrated Source-to-Sea (S2S) approach, the project enhances the ecological integrity, social well-being, and economic resilience of communities and Large Marine Ecosystems (LMEs) connected to Central America’s watersheds. The CAM Project supports livelihoods, improves human health, strengthens food and water security, and promotes economic opportunities linked to ecosystem restoration and sustainable resource use. Collectively, these efforts build climate resilience and contribute directly to the Global Environment Facility’s (GEF) “Healthy Planet, Healthy People” framework, ensuring that environmental recovery translates into lasting social and economic benefits for the region.339. At the regional and institutional level, the project supports the implementation of ERAM 2050 and its Agenda 35 by reinforcing policies and investment frameworks that attract both public and private co-financing for sustainable development. This will generate employment not only in environmental management but also in service industries that support ecosystem-based livelihoods. The creation of a Regional Investment Portfolio and financing mechanisms—such as water funds and payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes—will expand access to finance for producer associations, women’s cooperatives, and youth enterprises, enabling investments in sustainable agriculture, restoration, and circular-economy ventures. In parallel, regional training and diploma programs—such as the Watershed Management Series delivered by FLACSO and the Transboundary Freshwater Management Certification under IW:LEARN—will professionalize environmental careers and create a skilled cohort of technicians, data specialists, and environmental managers across the SICA region, advancing FAO’s Decent Rural Employment objectives of fair income, stability, and social inclusion. Training programs will address participation barriers including scheduling conflicts, transportation costs, and educational prerequisites that disproportionately exclude women and Indigenous communities from environmental careers. Recruitment will seek diverse participants across gender, ethnicity, and age groups.340. Under Component 2, the project generates green and blue jobs through integrated watershed and coastal management. The development and early implementation of 12 Integrated S2S Management Plans will engage farmers, fisherfolk, and community groups in sustainable land and water-use practices—such as soil restoration, reforestation, riparian buffer creation, and organic waste management—that improve productivity while reducing pollution. The installation of water-quality monitoring systems, laboratory upgrades, and citizen-science networks will create technical employment for youth and women as field monitors, data managers, and technicians. Strengthened basin governance committees will formalize participatory decision-making, offering stipends or contracts for coordination, training, and facilitation. Together, these interventions will promote climate-resilient livelihoods and reduce economic vulnerability in areas highly exposed to droughts, floods, and market volatility.341. Component 3 deepens economic inclusion by improving access to finance and market opportunities for sustainable producers. By designing financial mechanisms such as water funds, PES schemes, and public–private partnerships, the project empowers cooperatives and community enterprises to diversify income and adopt climate-smart technologies. These instruments stimulate demand for local goods and services—nurseries, ecotourism, composting, sustainable livestock, and recycling ventures—thus reinforcing rural employment multipliers. Financial mechanisms will accommodate diverse arrangements and address barriers women and Indigenous groups face in accessing formal credit systems. Technical assistance will support groups with limited administrative capacity. Participation requirements will account for time constraints affecting those with unpaid care responsibilities. 342. At the national level, project interventions will generate direct employment and diversified livelihoods across all participating countries. In Guatemala, the Sustainable Fisheries and Public–Private Action Package in the Sarstún and Dulce River Basins will train local cooperatives in legal fishing practices, enforcement, and alternative income generation such as ecotourism, aquaculture, and value-added processing—helping rebuild fish stocks, improve water quality, and stabilize household incomes. In Honduras, the Ridge-to-Reef Production and Fisheries Investment Model in the Manchaguala Sub-basin of the Chamelecón River will link sustainable agriculture and fisheries restoration, training farmers and cooperatives in regenerative and biogas-based production systems that reduce sedimentation and strengthen food security. In El Salvador, the Restoration Planning and Implementation Framework in the Lempa and Los Cóbanos Basins will train watershed committees, NGOs, and protected-area administrators in monitoring and restoration, creating jobs in reforestation, mangrove rehabilitation, and sustainable tourism. In Belize, training of local authorities and farmers in agrochemical management and nutrient-reduction practices in the New River and Hondo River systems will improve water quality in Chetumal Bay and sustain fisheries and tourism livelihoods. In Costa Rica, farmers in the Tempisque River Basin will apply sustainable livestock and precision agriculture techniques that increase productivity and reduce nutrient runoff, while in Panama, training for community-based organizations in the Tonosí River and Isla de Cañas systems will strengthen eco-business and blue-economy initiatives in fisheries, ecotourism, and recycling. Similarly, in the Dominican Republic, training on circular-economy models for small enterprises and municipalities will improve waste management, foster recycling markets, and generate new jobs in environmental services. Together, these activities will enhance productivity, diversify income, and strengthen community resilience across watersheds and coastal areas in the SICA region.343. Complementing these national initiatives, Component 4 expands the project’s reach through regional learning and professional development. Training programs such as the Wastewater Treatment Course delivered with Amigos de Sian Ka’an and the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana, along with the Watershed Management Diploma Series, will enhance technical capacity among local authorities, technicians, and environmental agencies. Through participatory learning events and knowledge-exchange workshops organized with SIWI, practitioners and policymakers will co-produce S2S tools and case studies. This bidirectional learning system ensures that local experiences from Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, and other countries inform regional policy, while synthesized knowledge from the Regional Environmental Observatory (REO) is returned to communities through accessible communication channels such as community radio, mobile apps, and local workshops. These mechanisms strengthen adaptive management, promote behavioral change, and build social capital across the region.344. Across all components, the project promotes gender equality and social inclusion as engines of equitable growth. Through the CCAD–COMMCA coordination mechanism, gender-responsive policies and indicators will guide implementation, ensuring that at least 40 percent of participants in training and governance structures are women, with targeted leadership roles for youth and Indigenous Peoples. Enhanced governance and social dialogue through watershed committees, regional networks, and CCAD platforms foster empowerment, conflict resolution, and collaborative problem-solving among rural stakeholders. The 40 percent target represents a minimum threshold. Monitoring will assess meaningful participation and decision-making influence, not only presence in activities. Indigenous women and youth will receive specific support addressing compounded barriers to participation. Anti-discrimination measures will protect all participants.345. By project completion, approximately 350,000 people are expected to benefit directly or indirectly from improved livelihoods, strengthened governance, and enhanced ecosystem services. These outcomes include job creation and income generation in restoration, monitoring, waste management, ecotourism, and sustainable production; reduced vulnerability through diversified livelihoods and better risk management; stronger social capital through inclusive institutions and community monitoring; and greater access to green markets and finance through certification, investment portfolios, and blended-finance instruments. The M&E system will track unintended negative impacts, such as increased women's unpaid labor supporting project activities without corresponding decision-making authority or income.346. The monitoring of socio-economic benefits will be integrated into the project’s M&E system (Outputs 4.3.1). Indicators will track beneficiaries disaggregated by sex, age, and stakeholder group, and institutional participation in governance structures. Progress will be reported in the Annual Project Implementation Reports (PIRs). Qualitative methods will assess changes in women's decision-making authority, time use, workload, control over income, and exposure to gender-based violence which are outcomes inadequately captured through quantitative employment metrics alone. Participatory evaluation approaches will enable beneficiaries, particularly marginalized groups, to assess project effectiveness from their perspectives rather than solely through externally defined indicators.347. The project advances FAO’s Decent Rural Employment goals by generating green jobs in agriculture, ecotourism, and waste management, and by supporting private sector engagement and blended finance mechanisms. Inclusive basin governance structures will be formalized (Output 2.2.1), embedding participatory processes and legal recognition. Though not a direct provider of social protection, the project enhances resilience through improved livelihoods, disaster risk management, and community-based monitoring. Social dialogue is fostered through CCAD platforms and watershed committees, ensuring rural stakeholders co-design land and water management strategies. Social dialogue mechanisms will create space for women workers, Indigenous laborers, and youth to voice concerns regarding working conditions, wages, and occupational hazards. The project links upstream communities with downstream coastal economies, supports diversified livelihoods, and enables access to green markets through certification. It improves access to environmental data via the Regional Environmental Observatory and ensures inclusive communication through analog tools and outreach, strengthening participation in sustainable development. Decent Rural Employment principles will explicitly address women's concentrated employment in informal, low-paid environmental work lacking social protection. The project will promote equal pay for equal work, prohibit discrimination in hiring and advancement, prevent sexual harassment in workplaces, and ensure that employment creation does not merely formalize women's previously unpaid labor without improving compensation or working conditions.
Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

To enhance environmental sustainability, economic prosperity and climate resilience in the Pacific Central American Coastal and Caribbean Large Marine Ecosystems through a Source-to-Sea approach that safeguards marine and freshwater resources for ecosystems and livelihoods.
